A boy has recurrent painful swelling of his knees and ankles caused by bleeding into the joints.

Which inherited bleeding disorder is most likely?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Recurrent haemarthroses are characteristic of haemophilia.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Iron-deficiency anaemia is not a bleeding disorder. C. Sickle cell disease causes painful vaso-occlusive crises, not bleeding into joints. D. Immune thrombocytopenia is acquired and causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding, not joint bleeds. E. Von Willebrand disease usually causes mucocutaneous bleeding such as epistaxis and menorrhagia rather than recurrent haemarthroses.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Haemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency, so it mainly affects males; spontaneous or minor-trauma bleeds into joints and muscles are typical, with a prolonged APTT and normal platelet count.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Boy, so consider an X-linked disorder ↓ Recurrent bleeding into joints (haemarthroses) ↓ Deep tissue bleeding suggests a clotting factor deficiency ↓ Haemophilia A
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, von Willebrand disease — the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, but it typically causes mucocutaneous bleeding such as nosebleeds and menorrhagia rather than recurrent haemarthroses.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Recurrent haemarthroses in a boy point to haemophilia, not platelet or von Willebrand problems.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Factor deficiency = deep bleeds (haemarthrosis); platelet disorder = petechiae and mucosal bleeding.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Reed-Sternberg cell on node biopsy = Hodgkin lymphoma; atypical lymphocytes = glandular fever.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient is about to receive a blood transfusion. Which check is particularly important immediately before administration?

options.A: Confirm that the patient has fasted for at least six hours
options.B: Repeat the group and save sample at the bedside beforehand
options.C: Confirm the unit has been warmed to room temperature first
options.D: Give routine chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone premedication
options.E: Bedside check of patient ID against the blood component

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Bedside check of patient ID against the blood component
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Correct patient identification and compatibility checking are essential to prevent potentially fatal transfusion errors.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Fasting is not required before transfusion. B. A new group and save sample is not taken immediately before administration; the bedside identity check is the critical step. C. Blood components do not routinely need to be warmed to room temperature. D. Routine premedication is not recommended.
live_plab_copy.pearl: The final bedside check confirming patient identity against the blood component and compatibility report is the single most important safety step immediately before transfusion.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Eliminate the options that are generic pre-operative or unrelated checks; focus on what is specific and critical to transfusion safety at the bedside.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: Candidates may overthink and pick an investigation that sounds clinically relevant (e.g. pregnancy test) rather than recognising that misidentification is the leading cause of serious transfusion incidents.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Most transfusion deaths come from wrong blood to the wrong patient — check identity every time.

akt_source.stem: A patient develops fever, abdominal pain and diarrhoea, which becomes bloody. They recently ate undercooked poultry. Which organism is a common cause?
akt_source.why_correct: Campylobacter is commonly associated with undercooked poultry and can cause fever, abdominal pain and inflammatory, sometimes bloody, diarrhoea.
akt_source.why_wrong: A. C. tetani causes tetanus. C. Cholera classically causes profuse watery diarrhoea. D. Giardia causes prolonged diarrhoea and malabsorption. E. T. pallidum causes syphilis.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient develops fever, abdominal cramps and frequent small-volume stools containing blood and mucus. Which organism is a classic cause of bacillary dysentery?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Shigella can cause dysentery with fever, abdominal cramps and frequent bloody or mucoid stools.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Cryptosporidium usually causes watery diarrhoea. C. Giardia causes prolonged, typically non-bloody diarrhoea. D. Cholera causes profuse watery diarrhoea. E. B. cereus can cause acute vomiting or diarrhoeal food poisoning but not this classic dysentery syndrome.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Bloody, mucoid, small-volume stools with fever and cramps mean dysentery, which points to an invasive colonic pathogen such as Shigella rather than a toxin-mediated or small-bowel organism.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Fever, cramps and frequent small stools ↓ Blood and mucus = colonic mucosal invasion ↓ Bacillary (bacterial) dysentery ↓ Classic organism: Shigella
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, Vibrio cholerae — a famous diarrhoeal pathogen, but cholera is toxin-mediated and causes profuse rice-water stools without blood or mucus.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Blood and mucus with fever means invasive dysentery; Shigella is the classic bacterial cause.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient develops bloody diarrhoea after eating undercooked minced beef. Which complication is particularly associated with some Shiga toxin-producing strains of E. coli?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli can cause haemolytic uraemic syndrome, particularly in children.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Guillain–Barré syndrome is classically associated with Campylobacter rather than STEC. B. Reactive arthritis follows Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter or Yersinia rather than being the characteristic STEC complication. D. Toxic shock syndrome is caused by staphylococcal or streptococcal toxins. E. Acute glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In suspected Shiga toxin-producing E. coli such as O157, antibiotics and antimotility drugs are generally avoided, and blood count and renal function are monitored for HUS, especially in children.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Undercooked minced beef ↓ Bloody diarrhoea ↓ Shiga toxin-producing E. coli ↓ Toxin damages endothelium, notably in the kidney ↓ Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, Guillain–Barré syndrome — a famous post-diarrhoeal complication, but its classic trigger is Campylobacter, not Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea after undercooked beef: watch for haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
